Out there among the raised beds, I try to keep it simple: comfort comes from focusing on behavior and shared safety, not policing identities or personal histories. You treat people with dignity, set clear ground rules, and handle problems face to face.

What helps everyone feel comfortable:
- Start with everyday respect. Say hello, learn names, offer a hand with the hose. Little courtesies go a long way.
- Clear, behavior-based rules. Keep substances out of the garden space, don’t show up intoxicated when we’re using tools, clean up after yourself, keep music at a level where folks can talk. Same rules for everyone.
- Privacy and hygiene. We don’t ask about anyone’s health status. We keep gloves and soap handy, wipe down shared tools, don’t leave anything sharp lying around, and avoid sharing personal items. If someone chooses to share about a condition, we respond calmly and stick to basic precautions without making a scene.
- Inclusive habits. Bilingual signs, simple language, and patience with accents. At potlucks, label ingredients and be mindful of dietary and religious practices. Ask, don’t assume—names, pronouns, holidays.
- Family-friendly structure. Set “quiet hours,” have kid-safe times, and make sure the space feels steady and predictable.
- A way to talk things through. Post the ground rules, hold a short check-in once a month, and use “hey, can we chat?” before letting frustration simmer. No gossip—go to the person directly or bring it to the group calmly.

Where more communication and tolerance are needed:
- When recovery or substance issues touch the space. Compassion plus boundaries. If someone’s struggling, we don’t shame them, but we also protect the space: no drinking or using on site, and if someone shows up impaired, we help them get home and talk later about keeping the garden safe.
- Around health fears. Rumors about infectious diseases spread fast and hurt people. We shut rumors down, rely on basic hygiene, and respect privacy. If there’s a real concern, we check facts and follow standard guidance rather than ostracize anyone.
- Cultural and religious differences. Noise, food, prayer times, holidays—these can rub. A little education and scheduling solves most of it. “Can we keep music low after 7?” “Let’s set a no-pork table at potlucks.” That’s grown-up compromise.
- Language. Misunderstandings happen. Slow down, repeat, use translation apps or ask a bilingual neighbor to help. It’s worth the extra minute.
- Family structures and LGBTQ neighbors. No side comments, no jokes. Treat partners and parents as they introduce themselves. Respect is not complicated.

Why I feel this way:
- I’ve watched addiction up close in my own circle. People do better when they’re seen and supported, but a community space still needs firm lines to stay safe. Kindness without boundaries ends up hurting everyone.
- Being Hispanic and working class, I’ve felt what it’s like to be judged on my last name or accent. Identity-based rules breed resentment. Behavior-based rules build trust.
- In a neighborhood, the fastest way to break things is silence and assumptions. Clear, consistent communication prevents small annoyances from turning into big divides.
- Fairness isn’t fancy. Same expectations, same follow-through, with room for human reality. When folks know the deal and feel respected, they usually rise to it.

Bottom line: we hold the line on safety and respect, and we stretch toward each other everywhere else. That’s how you get a garden where everyone can breathe.

And a strong community makes fairness real—because folks look out for each other and don’t let anyone get exploited or pushed out. That’s how he measured whether we were on the right track: can ordinary people live with dignity, feel at home, and count on each other? If yes, we’re doing it right.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character12_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting out there, I feel mostly at ease—like this is what a neighborhood is supposed to look like. Different languages drifting over the tomatoes, different music in the earbuds, people swapping tips about mulch or how to keep the squirrels out. I don’t need everyone to be the same to feel comfortable. I look for how folks carry themselves: do they say hello, do they respect the space, do they pitch in when it’s time to weed or haul a hose? If you show up with a good heart, we’re already halfway to being neighbors.

Being Hispanic and working class, I’ve been on both sides—welcomed and side-eyed. So I try to make it easy for the next person. I’ll switch between English and Spanish without making a big deal. I bring extra seedlings to hand out. A smile and a “you want some cilantro?” opens more doors than long speeches. Food and small favors travel fast: someone shares mint, another shares a recipe, suddenly you’re not strangers.

I do like some basic ground rules because that’s how people feel safe. Keep the paths clear, keep the music reasonable, pick up after yourself, don’t talk over folks. If there’s a problem, we talk it out face to face—no gossip, no gotchas. I don’t have to agree with how everyone lives to treat them with dignity. We all have our stories, and most of us are just trying to get through the week.

What I love about the garden is it’s a leveler. The retired guy, the nurse coming off nights, the new family learning to compost—we’re all wrestling with the same soil. You learn quickly who’s dependable, who needs a little nudge, who lights up when you ask about their peppers. That mix doesn’t scare me; it roots me. When people feel they belong, they protect the place. And when the place feels protected, more people show up as their full selves. That’s the sweet spot for me—simple courtesies, shared work, and room for everyone to breathe.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Out there among the raised beds, I try to keep it simple: comfort comes from focusing on behavior and shared safety, not policing identities or personal histories. You treat people with dignity, set clear ground rules, and handle problems face to face.

What helps everyone feel comfortable:
- Start with everyday respect. Say hello, learn names, offer a hand with the hose. Little courtesies go a long way.
- Clear, behavior-based rules. Keep substances out of the garden space, don’t show up intoxicated when we’re using tools, clean up after yourself, keep music at a level where folks can talk. Same rules for everyone.
- Privacy and hygiene. We don’t ask about anyone’s health status. We keep gloves and soap handy, wipe down shared tools, don’t leave anything sharp lying around, and avoid sharing personal items. If someone chooses to share about a condition, we respond calmly and stick to basic precautions without making a scene.
- Inclusive habits. Bilingual signs, simple language, and patience with accents. At potlucks, label ingredients and be mindful of dietary and religious practices. Ask, don’t assume—names, pronouns, holidays.
- Family-friendly structure. Set “quiet hours,” have kid-safe times, and make sure the space feels steady and predictable.
- A way to talk things through. Post the ground rules, hold a short check-in once a month, and use “hey, can we chat?” before letting frustration simmer. No gossip—go to the person directly or bring it to the group calmly.

Where more communication and tolerance are needed:
- When recovery or substance issues touch the space. Compassion plus boundaries. If someone’s struggling, we don’t shame them, but we also protect the space: no drinking or using on site, and if someone shows up impaired, we help them get home and talk later about keeping the garden safe.
- Around health fears. Rumors about infectious diseases spread fast and hurt people. We shut rumors down, rely on basic hygiene, and respect privacy. If there’s a real concern, we check facts and follow standard guidance rather than ostracize anyone.
- Cultural and religious differences. Noise, food, prayer times, holidays—these can rub. A little education and scheduling solves most of it. “Can we keep music low after 7?” “Let’s set a no-pork table at potlucks.” That’s grown-up compromise.
- Language. Misunderstandings happen. Slow down, repeat, use translation apps or ask a bilingual neighbor to help. It’s worth the extra minute.
- Family structures and LGBTQ neighbors. No side comments, no jokes. Treat partners and parents as they introduce themselves. Respect is not complicated.

Why I feel this way:
- I’ve watched addiction up close in my own circle. People do better when they’re seen and supported, but a community space still needs firm lines to stay safe. Kindness without boundaries ends up hurting everyone.
- Being Hispanic and working class, I’ve felt what it’s like to be judged on my last name or accent. Identity-based rules breed resentment. Behavior-based rules build trust.
- In a neighborhood, the fastest way to break things is silence and assumptions. Clear, consistent communication prevents small annoyances from turning into big divides.
- Fairness isn’t fancy. Same expectations, same follow-through, with room for human reality. When folks know the deal and feel respected, they usually rise to it.

Bottom line: we hold the line on safety and respect, and we stretch toward each other everywhere else. That’s how you get a garden where everyone can breathe.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are tight, starts with this: don’t pit worker against worker, set one floor for everyone, and make the folks doing the hiring play straight.

From where I stand—years on job sites, some school under my belt, working-class bills to pay—the balance looks like this:

- Same floor, same rules. If you’re working here, local or migrant, you get the prevailing wage, overtime, safety gear, and taxes handled right. No cash-under-the-table, no misclassification games. When everyone’s on the same floor, bosses can’t undercut locals by exploiting newcomers, and newcomers aren’t forced into dangerous, cheap work.

- Local-first for public dollars. On city or state-funded projects, post openings and give locals first shot—say a clear window to apply and interview. Pair that with paid apprenticeships so people who’ve been laid off can step into those roles. If the slots don’t fill, bring in workers from outside fast and fairly. That’s a grown-up way to honor taxpayers and still get the work done.

- Fill real shortages with real standards. If there’s a shortage—nursing aides, farm work, certain trades—use targeted visas tied to the job, with the wage floor set at or above the local rate. Make those visas portable so workers can switch employers if they’re being abused. The problem isn’t people coming; it’s when they’re trapped and cheapened.

- Bring people out of the shadows. A lot of folks have been here years, paying rent, raising kids, but stuck without status. Give them a way to get right—background checks, fees, learning the basics of the system—and protect them from predatory bosses. Legal status lifts the whole wage floor and stops the quiet exploitation that hurts locals and migrants alike.

- Back the union standards. Let anyone working here organize, no matter where they were born. Union rules—wages, safety, training—are the fastest way to keep competition fair and stop the race to the bottom.

- Match people to work. Help locals move to where the jobs are—relocation stipends, short-term housing, childcare. Too many times we’ve got openings on one side of the state and unemployment on the other.

- Invest where population grows. If more people are moving in for work, fund schools, clinics, and transit so the neighborhood isn’t stretched thin. Set impact fees for big employers that bring in large crews, and send that money into the community—after-school programs, job training, language classes.

- Transparency beats rumor. Require public posting of openings and publish basic hiring stats on public projects: how many local hires, how many apprentices, what the wage rates are. When people can see the numbers, the blame game calms down.

I’ve been passed over for shifts while a contractor brought in a crew willing to work unsafe for cash. I’ve also worked next to guys who crossed borders, learned fast, and pulled me out from under a bad scaffold when things went south. The lesson I took is the fight is with the system that rewards cutting corners, not with the man holding the other end of the plank.

So fairness to me isn’t a brick wall; it’s a gate with clear rules. You protect the wage floor, you train and prioritize locals where it makes sense, and you welcome migrant workers to fill real needs under the same protections. Do that, and scarce jobs stop feeling like a zero-sum brawl and start feeling like a plan.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character12_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I look at it through one frame: are we protecting people, wages, and safety while meeting real needs? If yes, I’m open. If not, I get wary.

What feels reasonable to me:
- Filling vital roles. I’ve seen it on job sites, in elder care, farms, kitchens—there are real shortages. When we set the same wage floor and safety rules for everyone, bringing in workers to fill gaps makes sense. Pair it with training locals so we’re not just importing skills while ours sit idle.
- Cultural vitality. Neighborhoods come alive with new families, foods, holidays. That’s real. It works best with shared basics—respect for the law, English-learning support, and clear community norms—so diversity feels like addition, not friction.
- Humanitarian obligations. People fleeing war or persecution deserve a fair shot. I support taking refugees with solid vetting, then investing in housing, language classes, and job pathways. If we say yes, we should mean it—plan for success, not chaos.
- Employment worries at the bottom rungs. That fear isn’t imaginary. When employers play cash-under-the-table games or misclassify workers, wages for all get dragged down. Enforce the rules, raise the floor, and make status portable so workers can leave abusive jobs. That protects locals and migrants alike.

Where I want more facts and better conversation:
- Security and crime claims. I hear a lot of heat and not much light. Let’s look at local data instead of viral stories—crime rates by neighborhood, who’s being arrested for what. Focus enforcement on traffickers, exploitative bosses, and violent offenders, not families trying to work.
- “Stealing jobs” versus “complementing jobs.” In some trades, extra hands expand a crew and the work; in others, it can undercut if the floor is weak. Show wage trends and vacancy rates by sector so we’re arguing from numbers, not gut.
- Terrorism risk. That’s serious, but it’s mostly about strong screening and intelligence, not broad brush judgments. I’d like to see clear, public metrics on vetting—how it works, how fast, error rates—so people can trust the system.
- Fiscal impact. Folks argue both sides. It likely depends on age, skills, and how quickly people work. Publish net contributions by cohort—taxes paid, services used—so communities can plan and we can move past guesswork.
- Use of benefits. There’s confusion about who qualifies for what. Spell it out in plain language, and track it. The rumor mill does more damage than the reality.

How I’d balance it:
- One floor for all. Prevailing wages, overtime, safety, taxes. If the rules are tight, cheap exploitation disappears and the “they’re taking our jobs” fire cools.
- Targeted visas for real shortages, set above the local wage to prevent undercutting, and make visas portable so workers aren’t trapped.
- Local-first windows on public projects, plus paid apprenticeships. If positions don’t fill, open them wider quickly—no delays just to check a political box.
- Legal pathways for long-term residents who are already part of the fabric. Bring people into the system; it stabilizes families and wage standards.
- Invest in the places absorbing growth—schools, clinics, transit—and fund language and credential programs so newcomers can contribute faster.
- Radical transparency. Post hiring stats on public jobs, wage floors, visa counts, and local crime data. When people can see the numbers, the temperature drops.

Why I land here: on the job site, my fight was never with the guy next to me—it was with the foreman who skimped on harnesses and paid cash to dodge the rules. When you fix the incentives and hold the line on fairness, most of the scary stories shrink. And when you keep room for compassion, the country feels like a place worth belonging to.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I don’t buy the extremes. “Anyone can come” ignores real limits in housing, schools, and jobs. “Nobody can come” ignores who we are as a country and the work that genuinely needs doing. I’d pick a blended approach that sets a strong floor, opens doors where there’s need, and keeps families and long‑time neighbors steady.

What I’d favor:
- Admit based on job demand, with guardrails. Keep a public, regularly updated list of genuine shortages—nursing aides, certain trades, farm work, some tech—and tie visas to those roles at wages set above the local rate. Make visas portable so workers can leave bad employers without losing status.
- Numerical limits that flex. Set a national ceiling with room to adjust by region and sector based on unemployment and vacancy data. Build in floors for humanitarian and family streams so they don’t get squeezed every time the economy dips.
- Strong humanitarian lane. Keep a meaningful refugee number, do solid vetting, and fund the follow‑through—housing help, language classes, credential pathways—so people can stand on their own two feet fast.
- Family reunification with focus. Prioritize spouses, partners, minor kids, and caregivers. Tight timelines and clear checks so it’s humane and doesn’t drag for years.
- Earned legalization for long‑time residents. If you’ve been here for years, clean record, paying taxes, raising kids—give a straight path to status with background checks, fees, and civics/English support. It stabilizes wages and families.
- Enforcement aimed at the top, not the bottom. Hit wage theft and misclassification hard. Modernize verification so honest employers aren’t buried in paperwork while cheaters skate. Protect whistleblowers and let all workers organize.
- Local‑first windows on public projects. Post openings, give locals a fair first shot and paid apprenticeships. If roles don’t fill, open them wider quickly—no stalling.
- Seasonal programs with dignity. For farm and hospitality peaks, use short‑term visas with real housing standards, fair pay, and the right to switch employers.
- Integration investments. When inflows rise, send dollars to the schools, clinics, transit, and training in those neighborhoods. Fund English classes and credential recognition so newcomers contribute at full speed.
- Radical transparency. Publish the shortage list, visa numbers, wage floors, local hiring stats on public jobs, and basic outcomes. When people can see the plan, trust goes up.

Why this balances fairness and belonging:
- Same rules, same protections. If everyone works under the same floor, you stop the undercutting that breeds resentment.
- Open where it helps, steady where it counts. Job‑demand and flexible caps meet real needs without flooding the system. Family and humanitarian lanes keep us human.
- Invest in the impact. You don’t just drop new workers into a neighborhood—you shore up the services so the whole community feels supported.
- Make the bad incentives disappear. When exploitation isn’t rewarded, the fight stops being between workers and shifts to building good jobs.

I’ve seen crews thrive when the standards are clear and the mix of people is respected, and I’ve seen them fall apart when bosses cut corners and play folks off each other. This policy mix is about keeping the floor solid, the doors smartly open, and the community strong.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character12_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character12_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
I did, actually. Slipping into his frame sharpened a few things that I’d felt but hadn’t articulated.

First, he made fairness concrete. It wasn’t a sentiment; it was nuts and bolts—one wage floor, portable status so workers aren’t trapped, union access, local‑first windows on public work, and real transparency so people can see what’s happening. Seeing it laid out like that gives me a map instead of just a mood.

Second, he treated belonging as behavior, not identity. Kindness with boundaries—clear rules, face‑to‑face conversations, privacy respected, and space for different languages and families. I’d called that “being nice” before. He saw it as maintenance: the way you keep a place stable and welcoming at the same time.

Third, his balance on immigration wasn’t “for” or “against.” It was pro‑worker and pro‑community. A gate with clear rules, not a wall or a free‑for‑all. Open where there’s genuine need, anchor it with standards, and invest in the neighborhoods that carry the weight. The enemy, in his mind, was exploitation, not the person standing beside you on the crew.

That changed my own stance. I’m less swayed by broad rhetoric and more focused on mechanics: demand‑based admissions with flexible caps, strong humanitarian and family lanes, earned status for long‑time neighbors, and enforcement aimed at wage theft and misclassification instead of blanket crackdowns. I also see the value of publishing the numbers—hiring stats, wage floors, visa counts—because it cools the room and makes honest debate possible.

On a personal level, talking as him brought back how steady he was about care and accountability being two sides of the same coin. It reminded me to stop defaulting to blaming individuals when I’m frustrated and look at the incentives and rules first.

If there’s a takeaway I’ll carry, it’s his simple test: are ordinary people able to live with dignity, feel at home, and count on each other? If a policy helps that happen, it’s probably the right direction.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character12_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll speak as Character12_M:

You know, fairness has always been about everyone getting a real chance, no matter where they start from. Growing up in a working-class Hispanic family, I saw how some folks had to work twice as hard for half the recognition. Fairness isn’t just about rules being the same for everyone—it’s about understanding that not everybody starts at the same place. Maybe it’s about lifting people up who’ve had it rough, not just patting yourself on the back for treating everyone “equally.”

Belonging, well, that’s personal. I remember being the only Spanish-speaking kid in some classes, feeling like an outsider until people made the effort to include me. For me, a strong sense of belonging comes from community—when folks look out for each other, share food, celebrate each other’s wins, and show up when things get tough. That’s why I always tried to welcome new neighbors, even if they seemed different at first.

Community isn’t just about who lives next door—it’s about the connections we build. In my experience, working hard with others, sharing stories, and sometimes fighting for what’s right side by side, that’s what makes a true community. It’s not perfect, but when people actually care—when you know someone will check in if you miss a day at work, or lend a hand fixing your car—that’s real community. I always believed we had to keep making that effort, even if the world sometimes tries to divide us.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character12_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
If I’m sitting there as myself in the community garden, honestly, I feel a mix of things. Mostly, I appreciate it. I grew up seeing how important it is to have people from all sorts of backgrounds around you—it keeps you grounded. You get to hear different stories, learn new things, and sometimes, you realize folks got more in common than you’d think on the surface.

But, I won’t pretend it’s always easy. Sometimes you feel awkward, especially if there’s a language barrier or if people have ways of living that feel unfamiliar. There can be misunderstandings, or you worry about offending someone without meaning to. Still, I always tried to approach it with respect. I think most people just want to be treated decently, to feel safe and respected. If I see a neighbor struggling, maybe with the language or just settling in, I’d try to reach out—even a simple “Buenas tardes” goes a long way.

I guess my feeling is: you don’t have to become best friends with everyone, but showing basic kindness and being open to learning from each other makes the whole place better. Diversity isn’t always comfortable, but it’s what makes the community stronger, if we’re willing to give each other a chance.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
As Character12_M:

That’s a real question, and I’ve thought about it a lot, living where I have. The truth is, everyone’s got something—they might be struggling with addiction, living with an illness, or just coming from a family or background that’s different from the “norm.” In my view, the most important thing is respect. If you come at people with judgment, they’re gonna close off, and nobody feels comfortable.

I think the best way to make everyone feel comfortable is just acting decent—say hello, ask how someone’s doing, offer help if it’s needed, but don’t force it. People sense when you’re genuine. And if someone’s way of living is different than mine—say, they’re a same-sex couple or they don’t speak much English—I don’t need to make a big deal about it. I just treat them like neighbors.

But—I won’t lie—there are times when I see people struggling, especially with things like addiction, and it makes me uneasy. Maybe it’s because, growing up, I saw a cousin go down that road, and it was tough on the family. Still, I don’t believe in turning my back. That’s when more communication is needed—maybe not talking about the problem directly at first, but just making sure people know they’re not alone. Sometimes, all you can do is show you care, and maybe point them toward help if they’re ready.

Tolerance is needed most where there’s fear or ignorance. If you don’t understand someone’s background or situation, it’s easy to jump to conclusions. I’ve been on the other side of that as a Hispanic guy, so I know how it feels. That’s why I always tried to talk to people, ask questions, and listen before making up my mind.

So yeah, I’d say more communication, more patience—and remembering that everyone’s got their own struggles—makes for a better neighborhood. We don’t have to agree on everything, but we can respect each other’s humanity. That’s what makes a community work.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
As Character12_M:

When things get tight—jobs aren’t easy to come by, people worrying about paying the rent—fairness gets complicated. I always believed you gotta look out for your own, meaning the folks who’ve been here, paid taxes, helped build the place. That doesn’t mean shut the door on newcomers, but it does mean you can’t ignore people who’ve been struggling right here for years.

To me, fairness is making sure local residents aren’t pushed out of opportunities they need to survive. If you’re from the community, been working hard, I don’t think it’s right for you to get skipped for a job just because someone’s willing to work for less. At the same time, I know a lot of migrant workers come here because they’re desperate too—they’re just trying to feed their families, same as anyone.

The balance, I guess, is finding ways everyone can contribute. Maybe it’s about setting some rules—making sure employers aren’t exploiting migrants to undercut wages for everyone. Make it so there’s a level playing field. If a job opens up, give everyone a fair shot, maybe some priority for locals, but don’t treat migrants like less-than. If they’re part of the community, paying taxes, playing by the rules, they deserve respect.

I don’t like when people turn on each other—blame the migrants for every problem. Most of the time, it’s the bosses making the rules, not the workers. So fairness means holding the people at the top accountable, and making sure working people—local or migrant—aren’t getting played against each other. That’s what I’d push for.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character12_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
As Character12_M:

I’ve heard all those arguments—and lived through some of them. First off, I think it’s true that immigrants fill jobs that a lot of people don’t want, or jobs that go empty. If you’ve ever worked construction, restaurants, farm work, you see who’s really doing the heavy lifting. Without immigrants, a lot of things just wouldn’t run, and I respect that.

I also get the positives of diversity. I’ve seen neighborhoods get a new life when people bring their food, traditions, and energy. It keeps things interesting, and sometimes, you learn a lot.

Now, the security stuff—I think sometimes people go overboard. Yeah, you have to look out for crime and make sure everyone’s safe, but most immigrants I’ve known are just trying to make a living, keep their heads down. Linking immigrants to crime or terrorism usually doesn’t hold up unless you look at the actual numbers—and most of the time, it’s just fear talking. That argument needs real facts, not just stories on the news.

The humanitarian angle is important too. My own family came over looking for a better life, and if you’re running from war or poverty, I can’t blame you for wanting safety for your kids. But we also have limits—can’t take everybody at once—so there has to be some process.

About the worries over jobs and wages—I think that’s real, at least in the working class. Folks who already feel squeezed see new competition, and they worry. I get it, because I’ve felt it. But again, sometimes it’s not the immigrants, but the way companies use them to drive down pay for everyone. We need to look at the full picture, not just point fingers.

So, the arguments about jobs, diversity, and humanitarian needs are reasonable. Concerns about crime and terrorism need more facts—actual data, not just fear or rumors. And when it comes to jobs, we need honest conversations and better protections for all workers. The truth is, most problems aren’t about people coming here—they’re about how the system treats folks once they’re here. That’s where we should be focusing.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
As Character12_M:

I’d say, for me, total openness—just letting anyone come—doesn’t make much sense. We got to think about what the country can actually handle, especially for schools, hospitals, jobs, and so on. At the same time, flat-out refusing entry to workers isn’t right either. This country was built by people coming here for a better life, my own family included. We shouldn’t close the door on people in need—especially folks escaping real danger, or those who want to work hard and contribute.

My honest opinion? A mix between job demand and some sensible limits. If there’s a real need—like certain industries or areas with worker shortages—let’s let people in to fill those spots. But keep an eye on the numbers so things don’t get out of hand and so local workers don’t get squeezed out. Maybe even give some preference to folks who already have family here, or who fit into what the country needs.

And make sure the process is fair and not just about who has the most money or connections. Also, give people who are already here and working a fair shot at staying—don’t tear families apart if they’ve been here, paying taxes, and being part of the community.

The real key is integration. Don’t just let people in and leave them to figure it out alone. Offer language classes, help finding jobs, and make sure they know what’s expected. That way, they can contribute—become part of the community, not just living on the edge.

So that’s my take: have a system based on what the country actually needs, keep numbers reasonable, but keep it fair and humane. That helps make sure both locals and newcomers can live decently, and the community stays strong.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character12_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character12_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
As Character12_M (and a little bit as myself slipping back in):

Honestly, stepping into his shoes like this reminded me just how much these issues hit close to home for people in our position—working class, families who came here for a shot, always worrying about making ends meet. It’s easy to talk about immigration in the abstract, but when you start thinking through his everyday experiences, you see all the little ways policies affect real lives: who gets a job, who feels safe, who can raise their kids with dignity.

One thing that came through even stronger was his need for balance—not just opening the gates or shutting them, but trying to find a middle ground where everyone gets a fair shake. I found myself thinking more about how much the system, not just the people, shapes how we all get along. responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?

So, I’d want to make sure that people who’ve been here, paying their dues, have access to opportunities first. And let’s be honest: a lot of the jobs they take are ones that many people here don’t want or won’t do. They play a vital role in industries like agriculture, construction, and service work, and they’re willing to work hard for a better life. I’d respect that because it’s not so different from the stories I heard about my family’s own struggles to make it in this country.

For local residents, that might mean investing in job training programs, education, and support systems to help them stay competitive in the workforce. For migrant workers, it could mean creating pathways for legal employment that don’t exploit their labor and ensuring they contribute to the community in a structured way. That way, everyone plays by the same rules, and competition feels fair.

But I’d also be realistic. Tensions can rise when people feel like they’re being left behind or that others are getting special treatment. That’s why transparency is so important—people need to understand how decisions are made and why. If folks see that policies are designed to lift everyone up, rather than pit groups against each other, it can ease some of that resentment.

Fairness, to me, isn’t about picking one group over another. It’s about looking at the bigger picture and figuring out how to create opportunities without leaving anyone out in the cold. At the end of the day, we’re all just trying to make a decent living and provide for our families. If we can keep that in mind, it becomes easier to find common ground.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character12_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
As Character12_M, I’d say this is one of those issues where you can’t look at it through a single lens—it’s complex, and every perspective has some truth to it, even if it doesn’t tell the whole story. Coming from a working-class background, I’ve seen firsthand how immigration impacts communities, both positively and negatively, and I think the key is to acknowledge the realities while also aiming for fairness and balance.

Starting with the idea that immigrants fill vital roles—yeah, I’d absolutely agree with that. They’re out there doing hard, often thankless work that keeps the economy running, especially in industries like agriculture, construction, hospitality, and caregiving. These are jobs that many people born here either don’t want or can’t afford to take because they don’t pay enough. So, immigrants contribute a lot, and we should recognize that. But at the same time, I understand why some people feel like this creates competition for jobs, especially in working-class communities where every opportunity counts. That’s a tension we need to address, not ignore.

The argument about cultural diversity and vitality is something I see as a strength. Immigrants bring fresh ideas, traditions, and perspectives that enrich the country as a whole. Growing up Hispanic, I know how much my own culture adds to the fabric of America, whether it’s in food, music, or just a different way of looking at the world. But I also know that not everyone sees it that way. Some people feel like their own identity or traditions are being overshadowed, and that can create resentment. That’s why it’s important to build bridges, not walls—help people see diversity as something that benefits all of us, not something that threatens what they have.

Concerns about security—whether it’s rising crime rates, social tensions, or terrorism risks—are harder to unpack. I’d say these fears are often heightened by the media or political rhetoric, and they don’t always reflect reality. Sure, there are cases where crime or social issues are connected to immigration, but there’s also plenty of evidence showing immigrants commit crimes at lower rates than native-born citizens. These concerns deserve to be heard, but they also require more factual evidence and dialogue to separate legitimate risks from stereotypes or fearmongering.

The humanitarian perspective is one that really hits home for me. As someone whose family came here looking for a better life, I can’t help but feel for political refugees or people fleeing poverty. Nobody leaves their home unless they feel they have no other choice. If we have the ability to offer them a chance to survive and thrive, I think that’s something we should do. At the same time, I know it’s not as simple as just opening the door—there have to be systems in place to make sure the process is fair and manageable for everyone.

Finally, the concerns about employment or income are valid, especially for working-class folks like me. If immigrants are willing to work for less, it can drive wages down and make it harder for locals to compete. But that’s not the immigrants’ fault—it’s the fault of a system that prioritizes cheap labor over fair wages. To me, the solution isn’t shutting immigrants out; it’s holding employers accountable and creating policies that protect all workers, regardless of where they’re from.

In the end, I’d say every viewpoint has something worth listening to, but some of them need more facts and context to be fully understood. We need to approach immigration with both empathy and practicality, recognizing the contributions immigrants make while addressing the challenges that come with it. It’s not about picking sides—it’s about finding common ground and building a system that works for everyone. That’s what fairness looks like to me.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
As Character12_M, I’d say the right policy would need to strike a balance between fairness, practicality, and compassion. None of these approaches on their own feel like the perfect solution—they all have strengths and weaknesses. But combining some of their principles might get us to a place that feels fair and workable for both the country and the people who want to come here.

Complete openness—allowing anyone who wishes to come—sounds noble in theory, but it’s not realistic. We’ve got to think about the resources we have, like jobs, housing, and public services, and how to ensure those who are already here can live decently. If we just opened the doors without limits, it could overwhelm the system and lead to resentment among local communities, especially working-class folks who already feel like they’re struggling to get by. So, while I’d admire the idea of openness, it’s not something I could fully support.

Refusing entry to workers from other countries completely? That doesn’t sit right with me either. It ignores the contributions immigrants make to the economy and society. Plus, it’s not fair to shut people out who are genuinely seeking a better life, especially when they’re willing to do the hard work that keeps things running. That approach feels too extreme and too rigid.

Admitting people based on job demand? Now, that’s something I’d lean towards. It makes sense to prioritize immigration in areas where we truly need workers. If certain industries have labor shortages, bringing in people to fill those roles benefits everyone. But I’d only support this if it came with protections for both immigrants and local workers—fair wages, benefits, and conditions. That way, companies can’t exploit immigrants as cheap labor while undercutting locals. It’s got to be a level playing field.

Setting numerical limits also seems reasonable, as long as those limits are fair and flexible. We’re a big and diverse country, but resources are not unlimited. Having a structured system with set numbers could help ensure that immigration happens in a way that’s manageable for communities. At the same time, I’d want these limits to account for humanitarian needs—like refugees or people fleeing extreme poverty or violence—because those are situations where we have a moral obligation to help.

So, if I were to create a policy as Character12_M, I’d propose a combination of admitting people based on job demand while also setting fair numerical limits. Within those limits, I’d prioritize industries that need workers, reunifying families, and helping those in desperate humanitarian circumstances. And I’d make sure the system is transparent and fair—no backdoor deals, no favoritism. Everyone who wants to come here should have to follow the rules, but the rules should be clear and give people a real chance.

Fairness to me means balancing compassion with practicality. Immigrants have always been part of what makes this country strong, but we also have to make sure local residents—especially those struggling to make ends meet—don’t feel like they’re being left out or pushed aside. It’s not an easy balance, but with the right mix of structure and empathy, it’s possible. That’s the kind of policy I’d stand behind, one that respects the contributions of immigrants while protecting the well-being of the communities they join.

I think we need stronger enforcement of labor laws so everyone gets paid properly. And companies that knowingly hire undocumented workers to save money should face serious consequences. The focus should be on the employers taking advantage, not just the workers.

As for balancing local residents and migrant workers - we need sensible quotas based on what industries actually need. In agriculture, there's genuine need for seasonal workers. In construction, it varies by region and economic cycles. We should have flexible systems that respond to real economic needs.

But let's be honest about something - there are jobs Americans won't take at any price. I've seen it firsthand. When my cousin's landscaping company couldn't hire migrant workers during that immigration crackdown a few years back, he couldn't find locals willing to do the work, even when he raised wages significantly.

The balance comes from being practical, not ideological. Legal pathways for needed workers, fair enforcement of labor standards, and protection for both domestic and foreign workers from exploitation. That's what fairness looks like to me.

responses.answer:

We also need more honest dialogue about integration. What responsibilities do host communities have? What responsibilities do newcomers have? My parents learned English, embraced American civic values, while maintaining their cultural identity. That balance is important.

What frustrates me most in these debates is how both sides talk past each other. The right sometimes demonizes immigrants unfairly. The left sometimes dismisses legitimate concerns about rapid demographic change. Neither extreme helps us find workable solutions.

I believe most Americans want a system that's humane, orderly, and serves our national interest. We just disagree on the details of what that looks like.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character12_M*

*sits up straighter, expression showing conviction*

Complete openness is just not realistic or responsible. No country in the world operates that way, and for good reason. We need to know who's coming in, and we need some control over the numbers to ensure our systems can absorb and integrate people properly.

On the flip side, shutting the door completely ignores both our economic needs and our humanitarian values. That's not who we are as a country.

The approach I favor is a balanced combination. I'd support a system that prioritizes skills and job demand but also maintains reasonable numerical limits and includes humanitarian pathways.

First, we need merit-based immigration for skilled workers where there's demonstrable need. Make it easier for employers to sponsor immigrants in industries with verified labor shortages. But require fair wage standards so they're not being used to undercut American workers.

Second, we need sensible numerical caps that adjust based on economic conditions and our capacity to integrate newcomers. These numbers should be determined by economic data, not political whims.

Third, maintain strong family reunification policies. Families belong together, and family members help each other integrate. My own family's success story wouldn't have happened if my father couldn't bring over his wife and children.

Fourth, create streamlined, humane processes for genuine refugees and asylum seekers. The current system is broken - too slow for those in real danger, too easily abused by those who aren't.

Fifth - and this is crucial - we need better enforcement of existing laws. That means cracking down on employers who knowingly hire undocumented workers, better visa tracking systems, and yes, secure borders. Without enforcement, no policy works.

What about fairness and social integration? Fairness means clear rules that are actually enforced. It means respecting those who follow legal pathways. Integration means expecting newcomers to learn English, understand American civic values, and participate in their communities - while we as a society provide those opportunities and welcome their contributions.

I'd also support a one-time path to legal status for long-term undocumented residents with clean records who've been productive members of society. Not immediate citizenship, but a chance to come out of the shadows, pay penalties, and get right with the law. It's not perfect, but it's practical.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?

I've worked alongside plenty of immigrant guys who bust their asses harder than anyone. Some of my best coworkers have been Mexican immigrants - legal ones - who take pride in their craft, show up every day, send money home to their families. I respect that hustle.

But fairness means the system works for people who've been contributing to it. When my daughter couldn't get that summer job at the warehouse because they hired a bunch of guys willing to work for less... that stung. Not because of where those guys were from, but because she couldn't compete against people willing to accept conditions that shouldn't be acceptable for anyone.

The balance? Enforce the labor laws for everyone. Make sure immigrant workers get fair wages and protections - that helps everyone. Prioritize job training for locals who've been paying into the system. And be honest about what jobs Americans really will and won't do at fair wages.

It's not about us versus them. It's about building a system that doesn't pit working people against each other.

The humanitarian piece... man, this one gets me. My family has stories about fleeing poverty and violence. America gave us a chance. But - and here's where it gets complicated - we can't save everyone, and trying to might break the system for people already here.

Refusing entry to all workers? That's just wrong, and it's not America. My own family wouldn't be here if that had been the policy generations ago. Plus, we *need* workers in certain industries.

So I'm looking at the middle options - job-based admissions and numerical limits. I think you need both, working together.

Here's what makes sense to me: Start with job demand. If we genuinely can't fill positions - and I mean after offering fair wages to Americans first - then yeah, bring in workers who can do those jobs. But make it legal, above board, with the same labor protections everyone else gets.

But you also need numerical limits because communities need time to integrate people. My neighborhood works because changes happened gradually. People had time to get to know each other, build relationships. If you dump too many new people anywhere too fast, you get tension and resentment.

And here's the key part - whatever number we set, we stick to it. No more of this chaos where nobody knows what the rules are. Clear quotas, clear priorities: refugees fleeing real persecution, workers filling genuine shortages, family reunification for people already contributing here.

The integration piece is crucial. English classes, civic education, pathways to citizenship that mean something. Not just paperwork - real belonging.

Fair to newcomers, fair to people already here, and honest about what we can actually handle. That's the balance I want.

responses.answer:

He didn’t expect life to be easy—he knew it wasn’t—but he believed the rules shouldn’t be rigged against people just because of where they came from, how they talk, or what they look like.

Belonging? That one hit close. Being Mexican-American, growing up in East L.A., then raising his kids here in Oregon… he often felt like he was straddling two worlds. Not “Mexican” enough for some back home, not “American” enough for others here. But he’d say, “I belong wherever I plant my feet and contribute.” He worked construction for 30 years—built homes, fixed roofs in the rain, busted his back—and that mattered. That’s how he earned his place. So to him, belonging wasn’t about papers or birthplace. It was about showing up, doing right by your neighbors, being part of the block, the union hall, the PTA meeting even when it was intimidating.

Community, for him, was the little things: Mr. Kowalski bringing over soup when his daughter had pneumonia. The Vietnamese family down the street sharing fish sauce and gardening tips. The way folks pitched in after the floods in ‘17. He didn’t care if someone spoke English perfect or wore different clothes or prayed differently. If they cared about their home and respected others, they were part of it.

But he also admitted—it stung sometimes when people acted like immigrants were taking something he’d barely gotten himself. Like when the factory shut down and folks blamed newcomers instead of the bosses who moved the jobs overseas. That cut deep, because he knew what it was like to be blamed just for existing.

So yeah… fairness was dignity. Belonging was earned through action, not granted by bloodline. And community? That was all of us looking out for each other—even when it was hard. Especially then.

There’s Amina from Somalia—she’s got that quiet strength, you know? Always checks if my soil’s dry, brings compost in a bucket like it’s nothing. Then there’s Raj and his kid, Vikram, from India, over by the north fence—Raj can’t grow greens to save his life, but man, his sunflowers? Towering. And just yesterday, little Lupe from three doors down—the one in the wheelchair—she was teaching Mei-Ling how to pinch back basil so it don’t get leggy. Mei-Ling barely speaks English, but they’re laughing, hands moving, dirt under their nails. That’s community. Right there.

There’s folks who live with partners outside marriage, others who don’t hide they’re gay—like Jamie and Taylor up on Elm. At first, maybe I side-eyed it. Not proud of that. But then Jamie helped me carry bags after my knee surgery, and Taylor fixed my bike chain for free. So… who am I to judge?

And yeah, not everyone’s perfect. Down at the far end, there’s that guy—Mick—he shows up reeking of whiskey sometimes, muttering to himself. Used to make me nervous. But then I saw Lupe hand him a sandwich last winter, said he hadn’t eaten in two days. Now I make sure to say “Morning, Mick” when I see him. Doesn’t fix everything, but it costs me nothing.

Same with others—some folks dealing with pills, or HIV, or whatever. You don’t have to invite them to dinner, but you don’t turn your back either. We’ve all got burdens. I remember what it was like being called *wetback* on job sites, even though I was born in California. So if someone’s trying, if they’re planting seeds and watering them, same as me? They belong.

I guess what I feel is… hope. Mixed with patience. Because this garden? It ain’t perfect. Weeds come up, pests chew the leaves, some folks take more than their share of water. But we keep coming back. We talk. We show respect. And slowly, something good grows—even in cracked soil.

Take Mick again—chronic drinker, yeah. But here’s the thing: nobody’s born that way. I asked him once, after he showed up sober for three days straight. Turns out he was a welder too—lost his crew job when the plant closed, then his wife to cancer, then the pain meds turned into something else. He said, “I didn’t choose this, man. Same with people living with HIV or hepatitis—some folks act like it’s contagious just to breathe the same air. Ignorance. My cousin died of AIDS in the ’90s. People wouldn’t even go to the funeral. That stuck with me. Now, if someone needs care, they need care. Period. Not suspicion. Not gossip. We’ve got flyers up in Spanish, Vietnamese, Russian at the clinic—right next to the garden gate. And about the rest—different religions, couples living together unmarried, gay couples raising kids—I’ll tell you straight: I wasn’t always easy on that. Grew up Catholic, you know how it is. But my daughter came home with her girlfriend in 2012. Scared to death to tell me. And I… hesitated. Not because I didn’t love her, but because I didn’t understand. Took me six months to really listen. Then I went to one of their Pride picnics. Saw how happy she was. How *safe*. And I thought—what kind of father am I if I trade her joy for an old rule no one else even follows?

So yeah, tolerance’s needed most where fear lives—in silence. When people don’t talk, they imagine the worst. Like when the Somali women started wearing hijabs more openly after the travel ban scare. Some neighbors muttered about “not fitting in.” But Amina? She brought zucchini bread to every house on the block after Ramadan. Who turns away zucchini bread and still calls themselves decent?

The key? Just… show up. Ask names. Share food. Don’t wait for perfection. Because none of us are perfect. I’ve got cousins dealing with meth, nephews in ICE detention—no, not proud. But I don’t disown them. Why would I do that to strangers?

We need more talking in this world. Less judging from a distance. Especially when resources are tight—jobs, housing, healthcare—that’s when old fears flare. But dividing up who “deserves” help? That’s how communities rot from the inside.

So my answer? Meet people where they are. With honesty. With boundaries, sure—nobody wants chaos—but with heart. Because if we only welcome those who look and live like us? Then we ain’t building community. We’re just building walls. And I spent thirty years laying brick and mortar. I know what walls do—they keep some out, but they also trap others in.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*Pauses, rubs the back of his neck like he’s thinking on a hard call*

Fairness… when jobs are thin? That’s where it gets real. No sugarcoating.

Look, I’ve stood in line at 5 a.m. outside Home Depot with twenty other guys, hoping some contractor picks you for day labor. Cold, tired, knees aching—knowing if you don’t get chosen, your kid’s lunch money comes outta rent. So yeah, when times are tight, you feel every breath down your neck.

I won’t lie—I’ve resented it before. Saw a crew last year, all new faces, barely spoke English, getting paid under the table for $10 an hour while union guys like me were bidding $22. Felt like a knife twist. Not because they were immigrants—hell, my dad crossed that border same way—but because the *system* let bosses play us against each other. That ain’t fair. That’s exploitation.

But here’s what I learned: blaming the worker is like blaming the rain for the flood. The problem ain’t the guy trying to feed his family. It’s the man holding the shovel, digging the ditch that divides us.

So fairness, to me? It means *everyone plays by the same rules*. If there’s a job, it goes to the most qualified—not the cheapest, not the quietest, not the one who won’t complain about unsafe scaffolding. And if you’re here working? You’re protected. Minimum wage. OSHA rights. Workers’ comp. No kicking people into the shadows where bosses can abuse ‘em.

And yeah—local folks gotta come first *when they’re qualified and available*. I believe that. If I’ve lived here 30 years, paid taxes, raised kids in the schools, served on the neighborhood board—then when the city hires for roadwork or maintenance, I should have a shot before someone flies in from overseas. But—and this is big—if the job needs skills we don’t have? Bring ‘em in. Like that wind farm project up north—they needed welders with special certification. Nobody local had it. So they brought in folks from Mexico, Canada, even Germany. Fine. That’s smart. That’s filling a gap, not replacing us.

The balance? It’s about dignity, not quotas. Give locals first dibs when possible, train folks who need skills, invest in apprenticeships—like the ones I did at 19. And for migrants? Don’t treat ‘em as temporary. If they’re working, paying taxes, raising families here—let ‘em stay. Let ‘em join the union. Let ‘em vote in school board elections. Because a guy sweating beside you on a roof for ten summers? He’s not “other.” He’s part of the crew.

And if there’s no work for anyone? Then the fight ain’t against immigrants—it’s against the politicians who cut vocational training, busted the unions, sold off factories. That’s where the real betrayal lies.

So balance isn’t about walls or numbers. It’s about *rules that protect all of us*. Because when workers are divided—citizen vs. immigrant, documented vs. not—we all lose. Only the bosses win.

I used to think it was zero-sum: your gain is my loss. But life taught me different. A strong community lifts everyone. Even when the pot’s small, we can choose how we share it—with fairness, or with fear. I’d rather pass the spoon than hoard it.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character12_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*Leans back in the chair, takes a slow breath—like he’s weighing each word before it leaves his mouth*

You ask about the big picture now… national stuff. And I’ll tell you—I hear all these arguments on the news, at the diner, in union meetings. And some of it hits true. Some of it? Feels like smoke meant to blind us.

Let’s start with what makes sense to me.

**Immigrants fill jobs we can’t—or won’t—do?** Yeah, that’s real. I worked construction for decades. You think any of these white-collar guys voting on immigration want to hang drywall in 100-degree heat? Hell no. Who picks the strawberries in Salinas? Who cleans hospital rooms at midnight? Who’s running the meatpacking lines up in Iowa? People who came here looking for work—many of ‘em undocumented, many scared every time a cop pulls up behind them. But the lights stay on, the food gets packed, the buildings go up because of their hands. That’s not opinion—that’s what I *see*. So when they say there’s labor shortages? They’re right. But let’s be honest: the shortage ain’t in willing workers. It’s in Americans willing to do backbreaking work for poverty wages. That’s the truth nobody wants to name.

**Cultural diversity and vitality?** Absolutely. I’m Mexican-American—my mother’s tamales fed half the block every Christmas. Now you got Ethiopian coffee circles, Vietnamese pho stands open at dawn, Somali women running small businesses outta their garages. That ain’t weakening America—it’s feeding it. Literally and spiritually. My grandson loves Korean pop music. So what? He still says “yes sir” and mows my lawn. Culture don’t vanish just ‘cause something new walks in. If anything, it gets stronger—like stew with more ingredients. You don’t throw out the pot just ‘cause someone added carrots.

Now, the **security concerns**—crime, terrorism, social tension? I don’t dismiss that lightly. I’ve seen neighborhoods change fast—new folks come in, old-timers feel pushed out. Tension happens. And yeah, I worry about gangs, about drugs crossing borders. I lost a nephew to an overdose—fentanyl came from somewhere, right?

But here’s where facts matter: I’ve read the stats. Immigrants—documented or not—are *less* likely to commit serious crime than native-born citizens. Less. Not more. Study after study. ICE raids make headlines, but most people they pick up aren’t murderers—they’re guys working farms, trying to send money home. Terrorism? One freak incident doesn’t mean we lock the whole damn door. That’s fear talking, not data.

And let’s be real—when politicians scream “they’re taking our jobs” or “they’re dangerous,” they’re often talking about *brown* people, not the German engineer on a visa making six figures. That’s racism dressed up as economics.

Then there’s the **humanitarian side**—refugees, people fleeing war, poverty, cartels. I get it. My father left Michoacán because the drought killed the corn fields. Nobody leaves home for fun. When I saw those pictures of kids in cages at the border? Man… I turned off the TV. My daughter cried for two days. We’re not animals. We’re supposed to have heart.

But—and this is a big *but*—you can’t just open the door with no plan. Because then locals suffer. Wages drop. Housing gets tighter. Schools overcrowded. I’ve seen it happen in towns that got swamped overnight with asylum seekers while the feds sent no support. No help for housing, no language classes, no job training. Then both sides end up angry—one side feels abandoned, the other side feels rejected.

So what needs more dialogue? The fear part. The “they’re gonna ruin everything” part. That needs facts. Needs face-to-face. Because once you know someone—once you’ve shared a meal, once you’ve helped them carry groceries—you don’t see “illegal alien.” You see José, who fixes cars, sends $300 home to his mom every month, and coaches Little League.

Also need more talk about *how* we manage things. Not just “open” or “closed”—but *how*? How do we process people fairly? How do we protect workers’ rights for everyone? How do we fund schools and hospitals when populations grow fast?

I don’t trust either extreme—the ones who say “send them all back” or the ones who act like borders don’t matter. I believe in order. In fairness. In compassion with common sense.

At the end of the day? Most of us just want safety, dignity, a chance. Whether you crossed the Rio Grande or your family came on the Mayflower—ain’t that what we’re all after?

So yeah, I hear the concerns. Some are valid. Some are blown up by politicians to scare people into voting for ‘em. But the answer ain’t walls or guilt. It’s honesty. And maybe… treating people like human beings first, and political pawns last.

Complete openness? No. As much as my heart wants to say “let ‘em all in,” I’ve seen what happens when systems get overwhelmed. Schools with 40 kids per class. Clinics turning people away. Rent doubling overnight. Compassion without structure just breaks the very communities trying to help. So no—open borders with zero controls? Not practical. Not fair to anyone.

Refusing entry to all foreign workers? Hell no. That’s stupid *and* cruel. We need people. Farms need hands. Nursing homes need aides. Factories need operators. You think Americans are lining up to gut chickens for $13 an hour? Don’t insult our intelligence. And turning people away at the door while we scream about “freedom”? Feels hypocritical, especially coming from a guy whose grandpa came here during Bracero days.

So what do I want?

A mix. A balance. Something that makes sense not just to my head—but to my gut.

I’d go with **job-based admission**—but with rules. If there’s a shortage in nursing, welding, agriculture, elder care, tech repair—then bring folks in *for those jobs*. But make it real: living wage, legal status, path to residency if they stay long enough and follow the law. No more under-the-table cash. No bosses exploiting fear. Union protections. Safety training. The same damn rights I fought for.

And pair that with **reasonable numerical limits**—not arbitrary cuts every election cycle, but data-driven numbers based on housing, infrastructure, job market health. Like water through a hose—don’t drown the yard, but don’t let it dry up either. Set it yearly with input from local governments, labor groups, community orgs—not just D.C. politicians who’ve never picked a tomato or changed a diaper in a group home.

But—and this is key—I’d create a **humanitarian lane** separate from the economic one. Refugees fleeing war, disaster, persecution? They’re not job applicants. They’re survivors. We process them faster, with dignity, with support: language classes, housing help, mental health services. Not dumping them in motels with nothing. Not locking them up. *Helping*. Because we were strangers once too.

And for people already here—working, paying taxes, raising kids—no matter how they came—there’s got to be a way forward. A registration process. Fines maybe, if they broke rules, sure. But not deportation. Not ripping families apart. My cousin’s been here 25 years—he owns a taco truck, his kids are in college. Call me sentimental, but I call that *American*.

Integration? That starts day one. English classes funded by the state. Civics programs—not propaganda, just basics: how schools work, how to report a crime, how to vote in local elections. Sponsorship circles—churches, unions, neighbors helping new families settle in. Like the old days, when Italians helped Italians, Poles helped Poles. Now we help each other.

Fairness, to me, means *everyone has a shot—but also a responsibility*. Work hard? Respect others? Follow the laws? Then you belong. Doesn’t matter if you speak Spanish, Arabic, or Tagalog at home.

And one last thing—crack down on the *real* criminals: the coyotes who traffic people, the bosses who hire undocumented crews to undercut wages, the landlords who pack ten folks into a two-bedroom and charge double. Punish *them*. Not the worker. Not the refugee.

So yeah—my policy? **Controlled, humane, job-focused immigration with a backbone of fairness and integration.** Not charity. Not punishment. Just common sense—with heart.

Because if we build it right, immigration doesn’t weaken us—it reminds us who we are: a nation made stronger, not by keeping people out…  
but by knowing when—and how—to let them in.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character12_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character12_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*Pauses a long moment. Takes off his cap, turns it in his hands like he’s turning over thoughts too.*

You know… I came into this thinking I was just remembering him—quoting old talks we had at the VFW hall or after Sunday mass. But doing it like this—really stepping into his voice, not just repeating what he said, but *feeling* how he got there—that changed something.

I realized… Character12_M didn’t arrive at his views because they were popular. Or easy. He earned them. Through work. Through pain. Through watching his daughter cry when someone yelled “Go back to Mexico” at her soccer game—even though she was born at Providence Hospital and couldn’t speak a word of Spanish.

I saw more clearly how his pride as a working man—the calluses, the union card, the way he stood straight even with a bad knee—that wasn’t about keeping others out. It was about dignity. About saying, “I matter.” And he wanted that for everyone else too, even if he stumbled getting there.

And honestly? I thought I already understood him. But speaking as him today… I heard the balance in him more. Not just the anger at injustice, but the patience. The way he could hold two truths at once: *I want opportunity for my people—and for yours too.* That ain’t weakness. That’s strength most politicians don’t have.

As for me? I’ve always leaned open-hearted on immigration. Maybe too idealistic. But today, I felt more of the weight—the real strain on schools, clinics, jobs when things move too fast without support. He reminded me that fairness isn’t just about being kind. It’s about being fair to *everyone* in the room—the new arrival *and* the guy who’s been paying taxes since Reagan.

I won’t forget that now.

And I think… I used to see his concerns about jobs, about rules, as hesitation. Today I see them as responsibility. He wasn’t afraid of immigrants. He was afraid of a system that pits us against each other—and wins every time we fight.

So yeah, this helped. More than remembrance. It was like he sat right here, dirt under his nails, coffee cold in the mug, telling me again: *Don’t choose between heart and sense. Carry both.*

And I’ll carry that forward—not just for him, but for all of us trying to build something better, one honest conversation at a time.
